```{r}
#Part A
universalbank1 <- read.csv("C:/Users/beanv/OneDrive/Desktop/Fundamental of machine learning/UniversalBank.csv")

head(universalbank1)
names(universalbank1)
dim(universalbank1)

set.seed(123)
train_index <- sample(
  1:nrow(universalbank1),
  size = 0.60 *nrow(universalbank1)
)
train_data <- universalbank1[train_index, ]
valid_data <- universalbank1[-train_index,]
nrow(train_data)
nrow(valid_data)
pivot_A <- with(
  train_data,
  table(CreditCard, Personal.Loan, Online)
)
pivot_A
#I created a pivot table using the training data with CreditCard and Personal.Loan as the row and Online as the column. The pivot table reports the number of customers own the credit card, using online banking activity and have the personal loan acceptance. For example, among customers who use online banking(online=1) and have the bank's credit card(CreditCard=1), the table show 475 did not accept the loan (Loan=0) while 57 accpept it(Loan=1)
```

```{r}
#Part B
loan_accept <- pivot_A["1", "1", "1"]
total_customers <- sum(pivot_A["1", , "1"])
probability <- loan_accept / total_customers
probability

#The probability that this customer accept the loan offer is approximately 10.71%

```

```{r}
#Part C
pivot_online <- with(
  train_data,
  table(Personal.Loan, Online)
)
pivot_online

pivot_creditcard <- with(
  train_data,
  table(Personal.Loan, CreditCard)
)
pivot_creditcard
```

```{r}
#Part D
p_cc1_loan1 <- 91 / (187 + 91)
p_online1_loan1 <- 179 / (99 + 179)
p_loan1 <- (99 + 179) / 3000
p_cc1_loan0 <- 792 / (1930 + 792)
p_online1_loan0 <- 1620 / (1102 + 1620)
p_loan0 <- (1102 + 1620) / 3000

p_cc1_loan1
p_online1_loan1
p_loan1
p_cc1_loan0
p_online1_loan0
p_loan0
```

```{r}
#Part E
numerator_loan1 <- p_cc1_loan1 *
  p_online1_loan1 *
  p_loan1

numerator_loan0 <- p_cc1_loan0 *
  p_online1_loan0 *
  p_loan0

probability_E <- numerator_loan1 /
  (numerator_loan1 + numerator_loan0)

probability_E
```

```{r}
#Part F
probability
probability_E
difference <- abs(probability - probability_E)
difference
#The estimate differ is approximately 0.34% so the more accurate estimate is from Part B. Because it uses the actual observed proportion of customers with CC=1 and Online=1 who acccepted the loan, which is given the result at 10.71%. While in Part E, we use the Naive Bayes assumption that the predictors are conditionally independent given the loan outcome.
```

```{r}
#Part G
library(e1071)

train_nb <- train_data[, c(
  "CreditCard",
  "Online",
  "Personal.Loan"
)]

train_nb$CreditCard <- factor(train_nb$CreditCard)
train_nb$Online <- factor(train_nb$Online)
train_nb$Personal.Loan <- factor(train_nb$Personal.Loan)

nb_model <- naiveBayes(
  Personal.Loan ~ CreditCard + Online,
  data = train_nb
)

nb_model

nb_train_prob <- predict(
  nb_model,
  newdata = train_nb,
  type = "raw"
)

matching_rows <- which(
  train_nb$CreditCard == "1" &
    train_nb$Online =="1"
)

nb_train_prob[matching_rows[1], ]

nb_train_prob[matching_rows[1], "1"]

#The Naive Bayes model estimates the probability that a customer with a credit card and online banking accepts a personal loan as approximately 11.06%. This result is matched with the estimate calculated from part E. Both methods produce same probability because they use the same Naive Bayes formula and training data.
```
